newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Germany, Austria, Italy to lift borders April 1998.
newsitem.headline: Germany, Austria, Italy to lift borders April 1998.

text.p: Borders will be thrown open across Europe from April 1 next year, German, Austrian and Italian heads of state announced on Wednesday after a late meeting on the Schengen open-border pact.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi and Austrian Chancellor Viktor Klima held a closed meeting for over two hours in the western town of Innsbruck to discuss the sensitive issue, which has raised German security fears.
"On April 1 1998 the last stage of lifting the controls will definitely come into effect," Klima told a news conference.
"This important result shows the population we take very seriously the freedom of movement within the Schengen region and the common task against illegal immigration and crime," he added.
This means that from April 1 1998 anyone will be able to travel from Hamburg to Naples or from Madrid to Vienna without having their passport checked by border police in the course of their journey.

Klima said Italy would become a full member of Schengen on October 26, which means it can do away with airport checks, but Austria will have to wait until December 1 this year to join the group, Klima said. Land travel will still be subject to controls until April next year.

France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Spain, Portugal and Germany are full Schengen members. Greece, Italy and Austria have signed but have not fully implemented the Schengen accord which introduces passport-free movement across European frontiers.

Germany has repeatedly voiced concern about Austria's ability to police its borders with Eastern Europe, raising the spectre of guns, drugs and illegal immigrants flooding into the country once checks are removed.
As a concession to Germany, Austria has agreed to lift border controls between the two countries step by step, rather than immediately.

Austria, on the European Union's frontline with the east, offers a perfect gateway for emigrants heading west in search of fortune and security. Its border with former East bloc countries is 1,260 km (790 miles) long.
According to a recent interior ministry report, Austria seized over 10,000 illegal immigrants in 1996, a rise of 61 percent from 1995.
Germany had also opposed early Italian entry in the light of the recent crisis in Albania which sent thousands of refugees fleeing across the Adriatic Sea to Italy.
Kohl and Prodi did not speak during the briefing. The three leaders are due to meet again at the end of this year to assess progress and ways of improving controls, Klima said.
Austria currently holds the presidency of the Schengen states.
